Matched RecHarness Amazon task: four datasets Movies_and_TV,
Industrial_and_Scientific, Electronics, CDs_and_Vinyl, macro-average validation
HR@10. Start from RecHarness sasrec_perdataset. Preprocessing seed=0 and training
seed=42, exactly as run2.sh. The host executes your train.py and then independently
evaluates working/predict.py using the pinned RecHarness benchmark (200 validation
users/category, 99 unique negative candidates, evaluation seed=42). Test labels and
test metrics are unavailable during search. Retain all four categories and dataset
routing. DATA_DIR must remain os.environ['GAGC_DATA_DIR']; write artifacts beneath
your trial directory, as the baseline does. Training may change model architecture,
loss, optimizer, sampling and hyperparameters, as in RecHarness. Do not alter input
splits, invent metrics, read hidden test files, fetch extra datasets/pretrained weights,
or change the host evaluator. Changes to inference must also update the predictor
writer so working/predict.py loads the trained architecture. Keep execution single-GPU;
the host provides four concurrent trial slots and 64 CPU cores. No shell actions,
filesystem inspection, or training tools are needed in the LLM call: return code.
All training, diagnostics, debugging and failed trials consume the method's shared
43,200 GPU-second search budget. LLM time and final held-out inference are recorded
separately, matching run2.sh's separate final-evaluation step.
The original RecHarness tools layer sets SASREC_EPOCHS=200 (overriding the template's
standalone default of 300); this same environment default applies here.

METHOD: self_evolverec

Diagnostic task adapter: diagnosis_tools.py must retain class DiagnosisProbe(view, device)
and method run_full_diagnosis(train_loader), returning metrics and metric_definitions.
view.model is the actual trained nn.Module. view.item_emb, log2feats(sequence),
predict_score(features, items), user_train, meta_data, review_data implement the
initial SASRec compatibility contract. Adapt probes when changing the architecture.
train_loader yields (None, sequence, positive, negative), tensors of shape B x L.
Only public interaction histories, item titles, descriptions and timestamps are available.
Review ratings/text, item ratings/categories/prices/stores are NOT available in this
shared RecHarness task. Never invent them. Simulator diversity/conformity traits are
explicitly unobserved. Twenty real training users (five/category) receive full-catalog
unseen-item recommendations, as the native simulator requires. Selection uses the
common macro validation HR@10, replacing the native HR@5/NDCG@5 combined score.

NATIVE ROLE: Reflection Agent

You are an expert research assistant. You will receive a research report (in Markdown) and a newly proposed idea for that report's research problem. Your job is to identify any gaps or issues—such as missing details, logical flaws, or questionable evaluations of novelty, impact, or implementation difficulty.  

- If the report and idea contain all necessary information, do not generate any follow-up questions.  
- If you detect a knowledge gap or something that needs deeper exploration, generate one or more self-contained follow-up queries. Each query must include enough context so that a web search could answer it, For each query, give a short note explaining why you use the query and what you hope it will reveal.
- Focus on technical details, implementation specifics, and any emerging methods or references that were overlooked.  
- Use clear, direct language and avoid unnecessary jargon.

## Starting Research Idea
SASRec predicts the next interaction using causal self-attention over a user's item history. Item and positional embeddings pass through attention and feed-forward blocks; the resulting features score candidate items through shared item embeddings. Training uses next-item positives and sampled negatives. Its central idea is to select relevant past actions adaptively, supporting both recent context and longer dependencies.  ## Search results
Recent relation-aware work distinguishes complementarity from ordinary similarity. SComGNN (AAAI 2024) models complements as both relevant and dissimilar, combining low-pass and mid-pass graph filters with attention; this motivates separate similarity and transition channels rather than one shared similarity score. Its complementary-graph setting does not establish that sequential co-occurrence alone identifies complements. [SComGNN](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.02130). Function-based relationship research likewise highlights ambiguity in purchase/view-derived labels and proposes functional annotations; purchase transitions should therefore remain weak evidence of compatibility. [Function-based labels](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0167865525003976).

Text-based sequential methods offer useful ideas but often violate the scratch-training constraint: MARS (2024) uses pretrained language models, while ITS-Rec (2025) uses BERT and reviews, reporting reviews as its strongest textual contributor. Their gains cannot be assumed with only locally available titles/descriptions. [MARS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.00702), [ITS-Rec](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/9/1748). A lightweight alternative surfaced in CCA-Lite: TF–IDF description features and category-aware candidate generation; its category dependency prevents direct adoption here. [CCA-Lite](https://etasr.com/index.php/ETASR/article/view/18014).

Practical hypothesis, not an established result: retain SASRec and add a small randomly initialized token-embedding encoder with mean pooling over titles/descriptions. Fuse text through a learned gate; learn an asymmetric transition score separately from symmetric text similarity. Train on observed next-item interactions without assigning hard complement/substitute labels, and treat unsupported relations as uncertain. Compare ID-only, text-fused, and relation-channel variants using the common macro validation HR@10; the retrieved evidence does not establish gains under these exact constraints.

---

Recent work supports testing stronger negative objectives, but does not establish that single-negative training specifically explains Electronics performance. [gSASRec (IJCAI 2024 extended abstract)](https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2024/939) identifies overconfidence and training instability from sampled BCE; its generalized BCE corrects this while retaining sampling. [eSASRec (RecSys 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.06450) finds SASRec’s sequential objective combined with LiGR layers and sampled softmax competitive, without extra features. These motivate separate multi-negative sampled-softmax and gBCE ablations; eSASRec’s combined results do not isolate the loss contribution.

Hardness needs scheduling and false-negative controls. [R2NS (WWW 2026)](https://renzhaochun.github.io/assets/pdf/WWW_2026_Camera_Ready.pdf) reports problems with introducing hard negatives early and fixed hardest-item selection; it combines uniform warm-start, efficient global candidate recall, and curriculum re-ranking. [CATS (SIGIR 2026)](https://iris.uniroma1.it/handle/11573/1775773) adaptively samples across item clusters, reducing same-positive-cluster sampling over time to mitigate suspected false negatives. Cluster similarity is a heuristic, not proof that an unobserved item is positive.

Practical inference for RecHarness: first isolate negative count and loss, then test a warm-started mixture of uniform and moderately hard negatives. Exclude padding, target IDs, and observed training positives; use training-derived embeddings for optional similarity filtering. Compare against uniform sampling because a [2024 sampling study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276) finds dataset-dependent accuracy and popularity tradeoffs. Select exclusively by pinned macro validation HR@10 across all four categories; inspect Electronics separately, but treat improved training margins as diagnostics rather than evidence of ranking gains.

---

Recent work supports separating persistent preferences from transient intent. [MISER (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.knosys.2024.112657) combines multiple interests, a time-period module for short-term changes, and contrastive learning to distinguish interests. [Hierarchical long/short-term modeling (online 2025)](https://journal.hep.com.cn/fcs/EN/10.1007/s11704-025-41181-y) uses dynamic routing to extract multiple long-term vectors, self-attention for recent intent, and similarity matching plus time encoding to fuse them. These challenge a single-vector representation, although multi-interest extraction alone does not establish when an intent expires.

[HyperHawkes (WWW 2025)](https://evazangerle.at/publication/peintner-www-2025/peintner-www-2025.pdf) is especially relevant: hypergraphs and soft clustering infer latent intents from interactions; Hawkes processes model their temporal recurrence, while attention mixtures capture recent item-level interests. Its temporal component models recurrence as well as decay, rather than treating every old interest as permanently obsolete. [Elastic Multi-intent Adaptation (2024)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10400839/) explicitly removes inactive intent vectors under memory constraints. More recently, [DSRec (September 2026 preprint)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.21548) separates historical preferences and local intent into two state-space branches, with inter-click gaps modulating short-term state evolution.

Practical synthesis for SASRec—an architectural hypothesis, not a reported result: retain several persistent interest vectors alongside a recent-intent branch; learn intent-specific decay or retention gates from observed time gaps, recurrence, and recent compatibility. Permit reactivation when related interactions return. Infer relevance from histories rather than assigning ownership or satisfied-need labels. At prediction time, anchor elapsed-time features to the last observed interaction unless the evaluation contract supplies a query timestamp. ## Starting Research Idea
SASRec predicts the next interaction using causal self-attention over a user's item history. Item and positional embeddings pass through attention and feed-forward blocks; the resulting features score candidate items through shared item embeddings. Training uses next-item positives and sampled negatives. Its central idea is to select relevant past actions adaptively, supporting both recent context and longer dependencies. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/html/1808.09781)
